Women previously convicted of, or cautioned for, abortion offences relating to their own pregnancies in the United Kingdom have been automatically pardoned, with details of their convictions, arrests and investigations set to be removed from criminal records. The pardon takes effect on Monday, November 16, following the commencement of provisions in the Crime and Policing Act 2026, according to a statement by the UK Ministry of Justice published on Sunday. The measure also covers women who were arrested or investigated over such offences, including those who ended their pregnancies or attempted to do so beyond the 24-week time limit provided for under the Abortion Act 1967. The ministry said some women had ordered abortion medication online, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, with some later saying they did not realise they were beyond the 24-week limit or had been victims of domestic abuse or coercive control. Under the new provisions, relevant details of convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations will be deleted from criminal records. Where complete deletion is not reasonably practicable, the records will be annotated and treated as though they had been deleted. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Davies-Jones said affected women would not need to apply for a pardon or take any direct action, adding that they could obtain further information online or contact the ministry’s dedicated casework team. The Chief Executive Officer of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service, Heidi Stewart, described the development as a historic change, saying women had faced investigations, prosecutions and convictions under abortion laws at vulnerable moments in their lives. “For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws – including police investigations, prosecutions and criminal convictions, often at moments of unimaginable vulnerability,” she said. Stewart added that although the pardon could not undo the distress experienced by affected women, it recognised the harm caused by their criminalisation. “Today marks an important milestone in ensuring that no woman faces criminal punishment or lifelong stigma because of the circumstances surrounding the end of her pregnancy,” she said. The ministry clarified that the reform does not change the Abortion Act 1967, which remains the legal framework governing access to abortion services. It said it would remain an offence for medical professionals or other people to act outside the provisions of the Act, but women acting in relation to their own pregnancies would no longer face criminal charges for abortion offences. Sections 241 and 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 provide for the decriminalisation and automatic pardon arrangements, with the latter provision coming into force on November 16.
